chapters.study-designs: Chapter 8: Study designs and planning methods

questions.question: Which description most clearly specifies a primary outcome for the chronic-pain trial?
options: Pain relief at four weeks, using a prespecified definition
Patient improvement at any convenient visit
Any outcome showing a treatment difference
The outcome producing the smallest sample size
questions.explanation: The outcome definition and measurement time point should be specified before choosing planning inputs. They are part of the Outcome component of PICO.

questions.section: Expected difference, target difference and clinical threshold
questions.question: A trial expects a 40-point difference, plans at 30 points, and regards 20 points as clinically important. At which difference is its stated target power evaluated?
options: 20 percentage points
40 percentage points
Every difference above zero
30 percentage points
questions.explanation: The target difference is the effect used in the power calculation. The expected difference and clinical threshold answer separate questions.

questions.question: What does a 20-percentage-point clinical threshold mean for a binary outcome in this tutorial?
options: Exactly 20% of patients will benefit personally from treatment
The event probability in each group must exceed 20%
A clinically important difference between the population event percentages in the two groups
Every treated patient has a 20% improvement
questions.explanation: The threshold concerns a comparison between population percentages. A between-group contrast does not identify each person’s treatment response or individual benefit.

questions.question: When should the study design and planned analysis inform the sample-size method?
options: After selecting the calculator that gives the smallest number
Before choosing the numerical planning parameters
Only after recruitment is complete
Only when a trial is statistically significant
questions.explanation: The question, outcome, dependency structure and planned analysis determine which planning method is appropriate. Reporting guidance helps document those decisions.

questions.question: What best supports the choice of a target difference?
options: A difference judged important and realistic using relevant evidence and clinical input
The largest effect reported in any small study
The effect that makes the recruitment target affordable
A standard value used for every disease
questions.explanation: The target difference should have clinical importance and a defensible evidence base. Its uncertainty belongs in sensitivity analysis.

questions.question: A Type I error probability of 5% describes which event?
options: Rejecting the null when the null hypothesis is true, under the test assumptions
The null having a 5% probability of being true
A 5% probability that any significant result is false
Missing a specified real difference in 5% of studies
questions.explanation: Type I error probability describes false-positive performance under the null. It does not give a probability that a hypothesis is true after observing the data.

questions.question: What does 90% power at the target difference mean?
options: The next study will estimate the effect with 90% accuracy
The alternative hypothesis has a 90% probability of being true
90% of treated patients will improve
About 90% of repeated studies under that difference and the stated assumptions would reject the null
questions.explanation: Power is the probability of rejecting the null under a specified true difference, design and analysis. Its complement is the Type II error probability at that difference.

questions.question: Two simulated studies use the same population probabilities and sample size but give treatment differences of 22 and 34 percentage points. What is the most plausible explanation?
options: The population difference must have changed
One of the two studies must contain a coding error
Random sampling can produce different estimates under the same population assumptions
The study with the larger estimate used a different target power
questions.explanation: Realized estimates vary between independently generated samples even when their population assumptions and designs are identical.

questions.question: A simulation estimates power using 400 studies. Approximately how many studies would halve its Monte Carlo standard error, assuming similar estimated power?
options: 400 with twice as many patients per trial
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo standard error is proportional to 1/sqrt(B) at a fixed rejection probability. Four times as many repetitions approximately halves it.

questions.question: What does 95% confidence interval coverage mean under the method’s assumptions?
options: 95% of individual patients have outcomes inside the interval
The true population value changes in 95% of studies
A narrow interval automatically has higher coverage than a wide one
About 95% of intervals from repeated studies contain the fixed true population value
questions.explanation: Coverage describes the long-run performance of the interval procedure under its assumptions. It differs from the spread of individual patient outcomes.

questions.question: A calculation gives 55.2 analyzable patients per group with equal allocation. What is the rounded analyzable target?
options: 56 per group, 112 total
55 per group, 110 total
56 patients total
111 patients split equally
questions.explanation: The required sample size is rounded upward within each group before adding the groups. Expected losses are handled separately.

questions.question: Under the introductory two-means normal approximation, what happens to sample size if the target difference is halved and everything else stays fixed?
options: It is halved
It doubles
It remains unchanged
It becomes approximately four times as large
questions.explanation: Required sample size is proportional to the inverse square of the target difference in this approximation. Halving the difference multiplies the requirement by four.

questions.question: What generally happens to required sample size when target power rises from 80% to 90%, holding other inputs fixed?
options: It stays the same
It becomes independent of the target difference
It increases
It decreases
questions.explanation: Higher target power requires greater ability to detect the specified difference. The normal-quantile multiplier increases, so the sample-size requirement increases.

questions.question: Why might the introductory two-means calculator and the reasoning lab return different planning results with matching inputs?
options: The larger answer is automatically the correct method for every design
The calculator uses a normal approximation while the lab uses t-test-based power
Both necessarily contain a programming error
The lab treats two measurements as two patients
questions.explanation: Normal approximations and t-test calculations handle sampling uncertainty differently. Methods and assumptions should be checked before comparing numerical outputs.

questions.section: Power at a fixed sample size
questions.question: A power curve holds the planned sample fixed and varies the true difference. What does it investigate?
options: How the original design performs under alternative population differences
Which effect actually exists in the population
How to change the target difference after seeing the data
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
questions.explanation: This sensitivity analysis evaluates a fixed design across plausible effects. It does not identify which population effect is true.

questions.question: After an inconclusive study, which assessment adds useful information?
options: Observed power obtained by inserting the observed effect into the same test’s power calculation
Selecting a larger effect to make reported power exceed 80%
Treating non-significance as proof of equivalence
The effect estimate and confidence interval, with design limitations
questions.explanation: The estimate and interval describe compatible effects and uncertainty. Observed power based on the same observed effect adds no independent evidence about the result.

questions.question: A design has 90% power at a 30-point benefit. What can you conclude about power at a clinically important 20-point benefit?
options: It is zero because 20 is below the target difference
It is irrelevant because the target defines the alternative hypothesis
It should be evaluated separately and will generally be lower
It must also be exactly 90%
questions.explanation: Power depends on the true effect. A clinical threshold below the target difference may have lower power and should be included in sensitivity analysis.

questions.question: A recruitment cap leaves fewer analyzable patients than planned. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Claim the original target power still applies
Evaluate attainable information and consider justified design or recruitment changes
Increase the assumed effect until the required sample fits
Ignore expected losses
questions.explanation: A resource limit does not establish adequate power. The original assumptions should remain explicit while feasibility and alternative plans are assessed.

questions.question: Which sequence describes a simulation-based power assessment?
options: Generate a hypothetical study, analyze it, repeat independently, summarize rejection frequency
Generate one study and treat its p-value as power
Choose significant datasets and average their effects
Increase the sample until the first significant result appears
questions.explanation: Repeated studies under an explicit model allow the rejection probability to be estimated for the chosen analysis.

questions.question: In a binary simulation, what do the specified treatment and control probabilities describe?
options: The exact event percentages that every sample will contain
The probabilities that the hypotheses are true
The percentage of simulations to discard
The assumed population event probabilities used to generate outcomes
questions.explanation: The generating probabilities define the hypothetical population. Realized sample percentages vary around them.

questions.question: How is confidence interval coverage measured in a simulation?
options: The average width of the intervals
The fraction of statistically significant trials
The fraction of intervals containing the specified true population value
The fraction of intervals excluding zero
questions.explanation: Coverage compares each interval with the known generating value. Rejection frequency and interval width measure different aspects of performance.

questions.question: What can explain a difference between simulated power and approximate analytical power?
options: A guarantee that the assumed population is realistic
Monte Carlo uncertainty and differences between the approximation and finite-sample test performance
Only an incorrect random seed
A guarantee that the simulation is wrong
questions.explanation: More repetitions reduce Monte Carlo uncertainty. They do not remove approximation error or establish that the model fits a real population.

questions.question: If 90 analyzable participants per group are required and 10% loss is expected, how many should be recruited per group?
questions.explanation: The calculation is 90 divided by 0.90, giving 100 per group. Adding 10% to 90 gives only 99; expected losses apply to the recruited count.

questions.question: An interval includes zero and clinically important benefits. What is a reasonable interpretation?
options: The treatments have been shown to be equivalent
No clinically important benefit is possible
The target power was necessarily miscalculated
The result remains compatible with both no difference and important benefit
questions.explanation: The interval shows the remaining uncertainty. A non-significant result alone cannot establish equivalence or exclude worthwhile effects.

questions.question: What is specified when planning estimation with a precision target?
options: The desired number of significant results
The probability that a fixed population parameter changes
A useful interval width and confidence level for the quantity being estimated
Only a p-value cutoff
questions.explanation: Estimation concerns the population quantity; precision concerns uncertainty around its estimate. Interval width at a stated confidence level can guide planning.

questions.question: What is an appropriate primary planning focus for a pilot studying retention?
options: Assuming a universal sample size applies to every pilot
Useful precision for retention and prespecified progression criteria
Definitive proof of treatment effectiveness from a small sample
Selecting the largest observed effect for the main trial calculation
questions.explanation: Pilot sample size should follow its feasibility objectives. Uncertain treatment effects from a small pilot should be interpreted cautiously.

questions.question: How should a small available population in a rare disease influence planning?
options: The team should increase the assumed benefit until the sample fits
The team can treat historical controls as interchangeable with randomized controls without justification
The team should assess attainable information and justified design options, potentially using collaboration or suitable repeated measurements
The team can assume the conventional power target is automatically satisfied
questions.explanation: Limited recruitment calls for realistic information targets and carefully justified design choices. Collaboration and efficient measurements may help; each option retains assumptions and limitations.

questions.question: A service improves its discharge percentage from 40% to 50%. What is the relative increase?
questions.explanation: The absolute change is 10 percentage points. Relative to the original 40%, the increase is 10/40 = 25%.

questions.question: Which report best supports checking a sample-size result?
options: Only the final total sample size
Only the name of a calculator
Only a statement that power exceeds 80%
The assumptions, evidence, method, allocation, analyzable counts and recruitment adjustment
questions.explanation: A reproducible justification connects the clinical assumptions, procedure and numerical result. A final count alone leaves the reasoning and calculation unclear.

questions.question: Two plausible sets of assumptions produce substantially different sample sizes. What should the justification do?
options: Average the answers without justification
Treat the larger answer as evidence that its assumptions are true
Report the sensitivity and explain which assumptions support the chosen plan
Report only the smaller answer
questions.explanation: The differences reveal uncertainty relevant to planning. The choice and its consequences need clinical and statistical justification.

questions.question: A fixed-resource study produces an interval from a 2-point disadvantage to a 15-point benefit. The clinical threshold is a 10-point benefit. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The treatment is equivalent to control
The interval still includes both disadvantage and clinically important benefit
The clinical threshold has been exceeded with confidence
The study rules out any worthwhile benefit
questions.explanation: The interval spans zero and the clinical threshold. Its full range should inform interpretation; an inconclusive result does not establish equivalence.

questions.question: The same Parkinson patient is measured OFF and ON medication. What matters for planning?
options: The paired measurements and their within-person relationship
Counting each measurement as an independent patient
Assuming the two groups are independently randomized
Using only the total number of recordings
questions.explanation: Paired observations contain dependency. Planning should reflect within-person differences and the intended paired or repeated-measures analysis.

questions.section: Units of randomization, measurement, and analysis
questions.question: A cluster-randomized trial already includes many patients in each of a few hospitals. With positive within-hospital correlation, which change would usually provide more independent information if the same number of additional patients can be recruited?
options: Recruiting all additional patients within the existing hospitals
Adding hospitals that can be independently randomized, with patients recruited in each
Recording the same outcome twice for every existing patient
Treating each patient as independently randomized
questions.explanation: Additional independently randomized hospitals provide new clusters. Patients within an existing hospital share cluster characteristics, so adding more patients there has diminishing gains in information. The final calculation still needs the cluster sizes, ICC, and planned analysis.

questions.question: What does a reporting guideline such as CONSORT primarily provide?
options: A guarantee that the analysis is unbiased
An automatic choice of target difference
Guidance on documenting and reporting the study
One universal sample-size formula
questions.explanation: Reporting guidance helps make decisions transparent. The sample-size method must still match the question, design and planned analysis.

questions.question: How can assurance differ from power at one fixed effect?
options: It always produces the same answer as fixed-effect power
It can average performance over a justified distribution of uncertain parameter values
It guarantees that the study will be significant
It removes the need to justify clinical importance
questions.explanation: Assurance or expected power incorporates a specified distribution of uncertainty. That distribution and the decision rule require justification.

questions.question: A study compares speech features for predicting medication state. What planning approach is appropriate?
options: Selecting the feature set with the best accuracy on its training data alone
A prediction-model approach addressing model complexity, performance and validation with patient-level dependency
An independent two-group mean formula regardless of the prediction method
Counting every recording as an independent patient
questions.explanation: Prediction objectives require planning for model performance and validation. Repeated recordings from the same patient remain dependent and should be handled accordingly.

questions.question: What is computational reproducibility in this tutorial?
options: Obtaining consistent computational results using the same inputs, procedures and conditions
Collecting new patient data and obtaining the same p-value
Using any software that gives a similar-looking plot
Repeating a calculation until the preferred result appears
questions.explanation: Computational reproducibility concerns checking the same computational work. Replication addresses the scientific question with newly collected data.

questions.question: Which approach supports open science for work involving confidential patient data?
options: Publishing identifiable patient records to make the study open
Withholding all methods whenever any data are restricted
Assuming a public PDF makes all computations reproducible
Sharing appropriate methods and code while using governed access or other suitable restrictions for protected data
questions.explanation: Transparency and reuse can be supported through protocols, code and documentation while respecting consent and legitimate access restrictions.

questions.question: What should accompany an exported numerical result?
options: Only the date of the screenshot
Only the rounded sample size
The inputs and procedures that produced it, with software and code versions
Whatever slider values happen to be displayed later
questions.explanation: A saved result should retain the assumptions and computational context used to produce it. Later changes to controls should not relabel an earlier result.

questions.question: Is saving a random seed alone sufficient to reproduce a simulated batch exactly?
options: No; random simulations can never be reproduced
No; the procedure, generator settings and software environment also matter
Yes, regardless of software or algorithm
Yes, provided the plot colors are unchanged
questions.explanation: A seed identifies a starting random state under particular settings. Different generators, algorithms or environments can yield different realized draws.
